planting.note: Root stolon tip cuttings in moist, humid potting mix; this gesneriad is the type species of Episcia and spreads by trailing stolons that root at every node. Keep night temperatures above 60F and humidity high.

directions: Grow in warm, humid shade in loose, peaty, well-drained mix, watering enough to keep the soil evenly moist without letting the shallow roots sit wet. Episcia reptans is a South American rainforest-floor species with metallic dark-green, faintly scalloped leaves and slender red stolons that creep outward and root as they go, forming a dense low mat within a season. Its orange-to-red tubular flowers appear sporadically among the foliage but are smaller and less showy than those of its better-known relative E. cupreata, making this species grown primarily for its spreading habit and foliage texture. It excels in terrariums, hanging baskets, and as a deep-shade groundcover in zone 10-12 gardens, but collapses quickly if air turns cold or dry.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC — Flame Violets (Episcia spp.)

planting.note: Propagate from leaf or stem cuttings in a gritty, fast-draining epiphyte mix; this slow-growing species stores water in its semi-succulent leaves and tolerates drying between waterings far better than overwatering.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered shade in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix, letting the mix dry out between waterings since the fleshy leaves and pink-red stems store moisture and rot easily if kept wet. Peperomia albovittata is a slow-growing Ecuadorian epiphyte whose species name describes its narrow, parallel bands of pale silver-green against deeper green on each small, pointed leaf, with contrasting wine-red stems beneath. It stays compact, rarely exceeding a foot tall, making it well suited to shaded windowsills, mounted epiphyte displays, or mixed terrarium plantings alongside other small tropical foliage species. The species is the wild parent behind the popular 'Piccolo Banda' trade selection and is itself increasingly offered by specialty growers.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online (Peperomia albovittata)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Peperomia species for indoor culture

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings directly in moist terrarium substrate or sphagnum under very high humidity; the fine, fibrous roots and tiny succulent leaves dry out quickly in open air but rot if kept constantly saturated.

directions: Grow in high humidity and bright indirect light over moist, well-aerated substrate, misting or enclosing the plant to prevent the tiny leaves from desiccating between waterings. Peperomia emarginella is a creeping Neotropical epiphyte or lithophyte found from Florida and the Caribbean south through the Andes, distinguished by minute, rounded, succulent leaves only a few millimeters across, each with a shallow notch at the tip that gives the species its name. The trailing stems form a dense, moss-like carpet over damp bark, rock, or terrarium floor rather than growing upright, making it one of the smallest-leaved Peperomia species commonly kept by collectors. It is best suited to closed terrariums, vivariums, or other consistently humid microclimates rather than open household air.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online (Peperomia emarginella)

planting.note: Divide clumps or root stem cuttings in moist, humus-rich soil; this Florida and Caribbean native tolerates more drought than the similar Pilea microphylla and flowers year-round in warm climates.

directions: Grow in moist, organically rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun, allowing the surface to dry between waterings once the plant is established. Pilea trianthemoides, native to hammocks and moist thickets of Florida and the Caribbean, forms a soft, ferny mound of tiny succulent leaves on multi-branched stems, closely resembling the more common Pilea microphylla but with slightly larger, more pointed foliage and noticeably better drought resistance. Its minute flowers release pollen explosively when triggered, the trait that gives artillery plants their common name, and it blooms nearly continuously in warm weather. It makes a low, textured shade groundcover or container filler in frost-free gardens, or an easy houseplant where winters are cold.
sources: Flora of North America — Pilea trianthemoides

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright indirect light; keep humidity high and use low-mineral water, as with other prayer plants.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light and consistently moist, humus-rich soil with elevated humidity, avoiding direct sun and mineral-heavy tap water that can scorch the foliage. Goeppertia lietzei is a compact, bushy prayer plant native to the humid Atlantic Forest understory of eastern Brazil, forming a clumping rosette of thick, oblong leaves with wavy margins marked by light-green chevron bands running from midrib to edge over a darker green base. The leaves perform the classic nyctinastic prayer-plant fold each evening and reopen with morning light. Staying under 16 inches tall and wide, it suits terrariums, dish gardens, and shaded understory plantings in tropical zone 11-12 gardens, and is the wild species behind several variegated marantaceae selections in cultivation.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online (Goeppertia lietzei)
